title: Whom shall I fear? (Psalm 27)
hookLine: the Lord is my light; one thing I ask, to dwell in his house

lines: IF YOU COULD ASK FOR ONE THING.
cards: One request. Not three wishes, not a list. One.
It's harder than it sounds: health, safety for the people you love, a little more money, the scan coming back clear, the person who left coming back.
Psalm twenty-seven is sung by someone surrounded: enemies closing in, an army camped around, false witnesses lining up, and he even imagines his own father and mother turning away.
If anyone has a long list of requests, it's him. And then he says: I've asked for one thing. Only one.

teach.b: Psalm twenty-seven opens, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"
Two questions, and they're not quite rhetorical. The psalmist knows exactly whom he could fear, and names them: evildoers, a host encamped against him, war rising up. The fear is real.
The questions are his way of standing up inside it.

Then, the one thing: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."
Not rescue first. Not victory. Nearness: to live close to God, and to look at his beauty.

Everything else, the psalm seems to say, follows from that one thing, or matters less without it. The fear doesn't vanish all at once. Halfway through, the psalm swings back to pleading: hide not thy face from me.

teach.h: WHEN MY FATHER AND MOTHER FORSAKE ME.
teach.b: Then a tender line: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up."

teach.h: WAIT, AND BE OF GOOD COURAGE.
teach.b: And it ends not with a victory but with waiting: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." Wait, twice. Two things worth knowing.
Jewish custom adds Psalm twenty-seven to daily prayer in the weeks around the High Holy Days in the fall.

teach.h: THE LORD IS MY LIGHT; WHOM SHALL I FEAR?
teach.b: And the first words in Latin, Dominus illuminatio mea, the Lord is my light, are the motto of the University of Oxford.

how: Some Christians pray Psalm 27 in times of fear, and it appears in daily prayer; in Jewish practice it is recited daily from the start of the month of Elul through the autumn festivals.

o: people lining up to accuse him with lies
prophets whose predictions never came true
friends who saw the truth but kept silent

games.q: what's inside Psalm 27 — tap the pairs.
p: to dwell in the house of the LORD

s: the psalmist says he has nothing to fear
he names real enemies. whom shall I fear? is courage asked from inside the fear.
the one thing he asks for is victory over his enemies
it's nearness: to dwell in the house of the LORD and behold his beauty.
Oxford University's motto comes from Psalm 27
Dominus illuminatio mea: the Lord is my light.

games.q: you're surrounded: enemies, false witnesses, even family turning away. you get one request. what does the psalmist ask for?
o: to dwell in the house of the LORD.
games.why: one thing: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of his life, to behold his beauty. nearness before rescue.

practice: Let your list of wants come up, big and small, then set things down one by one, like taking items out of an overfull bag, until you're holding just one. It may be close to the psalmist's, or something else entirely.
If you pray, ask God for it plainly; if you don't, just let yourself know what it is.

wordCard.voice: False witnesses. People lining up against the psalmist, one of the real dangers he names before asking for just one thing.

orig.note: Hebrew: one thing I have asked, from Psalm 27:4.

carryVoice: Your line: one thing I ask. Wait, he says, and be of good courage. That's day four hundred seventeen.
